# What is "spatial analysis"?

##

![[Source: https://www.census.gov/library/visualizations/2020/geo/center-of-population-1790-2020.html](https://www.census.gov/library/visualizations/2020/geo/center-of-population-1790-2020.html)](images/image2.png){alt="Map of mean center of US population"}

## Spatial analysis for social science applications

- Often we use spatial analysis tools to extract information
- Length of paved road in a region
- Number of universities in a place
- Number of inhabitants within a distance of a service
- Area within a distance of a road or feature (like a bus stop or metro station)

## Types of spatial analysis <br> (according to Longley)  {.smaller}

- **Queries and reasoning** – no changes are made to the database and no new information is produced
  - For example, how many cities within 300 miles of Providence?
- **Measurements** --- Describing aspects of geographic data, like length, area, or shape
  - For example, calculating the size (or area) of a parcel
- **Transformations** --- Changing or combining data to create new data
  - Using logical, mathematical, or geometrical rules
- **Descriptive summaries** --- summary statistics for spatial data
- **Optimization** --- Finding the best locations for a set of objects, given a set of criteria
  - For example, best locations for public services
- **Hypothesis testing** --- Making generalizations about a population from a sample
  - Could this spatial pattern have occurred by chance?

# We've covered queries and reasoning

## Measurements {.smaller}

- How far apart are two points?  How large is a parcel's area?
- **Area**
- **Distance** or **length**
  - Distance may be measured two ways:
    - Straight line or Pythagorean distance.  Also referred to as "as the crow flies"
      - Assumes a flat plane, for latitude and longitude we need to think of great circle distances
    - Manhattan or network distance
- **Shape** --- for example Gerrymandering
  - S=P/3.54√A
    - Where P is perimeter and A is area; 3.54 is twice the square root of π
    - S=1 for the most compact shape, a circle
- **Slope** and **aspect**
  - Digital Elevation Models or DEMs
    - Rasters whose cells contain the elevation at that location

## Transformations {.smaller}

- **Buffers** --- Create an area of a specific and constant width around a point, line, or polygon
  - This can be used to identify all objects falling within a certain distance of the original feature
- **Point in polygon** --- Associates points with polygons
  - Counts the number of points within a polygon or…Attaches polygon characteristics to points
  - This is usually what people mean when they refer to a spatial join
- **Polygon overlay** --- Determining whether two polygons overlap, the extent of their overlap, and what new polygons are created by the overlap
  - Can be thought of as an intersection or a union of units and information
- **Spatial interpolation** --- Estimating the value of a variable for locations where no measurement has occurred.
  - For example, rainfall, temperature, or elevation
  - e.g., Inverse distance weighting or Kriging
- **Density estimation and potential** --- generates a surface from a set of discrete points

## Intersect

What if we want to know areas where two (or more) layers overlap?

![](images/image12.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot"}

## Intersect

:::: {.columns}

:::{.column width="50%"}

\

- Only keeps polygon areas that were common to both layers
  - Makes it easier to identify locations where two conditions are in effect simultaneously
    - E.g. habitat identification
    - Or overlaps between census geographies (with pop data) and buffers

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}

\

![](images/image13.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot"}

:::

::::

## Thiessen (or Voronoi) polygons

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="40%"}

- Creating polygons from points
- What about the case where we might want to go from point features to polygons?
- For example, suppose we want to define "catchment areas" for metro station?
- The assumption being that each person will use the station closest to them
- How is this different from buffers?

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](images/image23.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot"}

:::

::::

## Thiessen (or Voronoi) polygons

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="40%"}

\

- Allocating areas to their closest points
- Creates new polygon layer as output
- Default extent of polygons is the bounded rectangle containing the points

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](images/image24.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot"}

:::

::::

## Thiessen polygon interface in ArcGIS Pro

![](images/image25.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot" fig-align="center"}

## Clip

::::{.columns}

:::{.column width="40%"}

\

- How to change boundaries of a layer to match another
- Clips—or cuts—one layer, using boundaries of a second layer
- Does not change the attribute table!
- So here, we can clip Voronoi polygons using the urban area polygon layer

:::

::: {.column width="60%"}

![](images/image26.png){alt="ArcGIS Pro screenshot"}

:::

::::

# Other common tools

## Near

Calculating straight-line distances between features

![](images/image31.png){alt="Example of how near tool works"}

Produces a new column in the attribute table with distance <br> **(in units of the projection)**

## Combining features from two or more layers

- Append and Merge ---
  - Layers must be the same feature type
  - And have the same coordinate system

![](images/image32.png){alt="Screenshot of ArcGIS Pro"}

## Converting polygons to points

- Calculating geometric centroids
- Summarizing an area (polygon) with a point
- Why would we need to be able to do this?
- Not to be confused with population-weighted centroids!

## Centroids

![](images/image35.png){alt="Screenshot of ArcGIS Pro" fig-align="center"}

## Summary

- So many more tools—this is just scratching the surface
- Most of these tools generate a new layer
  - Pay attention to naming AND to where you're saving!
- If you mess up, you can simply run the tool again
- Using Help and the internet is key
- It's common to need to string together tools to get to a final answer
- Layer names can matter:
  - No spaces or strange symbols.
  - Use _
  - No starting a layer name with a number (e.g., Pop_2011, not 2011_pop)
